longTermStarterPack.title: 5-7 Holding Long-Term Starter Pack
longTermStarterPack.philosophy: For a $10K account, keep it concentrated enough to understand but diversified enough to survive mistakes. Use ETFs as the foundation, then add only a few exceptional businesses that can compound for 10-15 years. Review yearly. Nothing is truly forever.
rules: Buy in 3-6 chunks instead of all at once if the market feels expensive.
Keep the S&P 500 ETF as the largest holding.
Do not add more individual stocks until the account is meaningfully bigger.
Review once or twice per year, not every bad week.
Sell only if the long-term business quality breaks, not because the stock is temporarily down.
criteria: Simple enough for a new investor to understand.
Durable moat: scale, brand, switching costs, network effects, or low-cost index exposure.
Financial strength: large revenue base, strong cash generation, high margins, or fortress liquidity.
Long runway: cloud, AI, digital commerce, software, payments, or broad U.S. earnings growth.
Portfolio job: every holding must have a clear role and not duplicate the same risk too much.
sourceNotes: VOO: Vanguard and ETF profile data show broad S&P 500 exposure with a very low 0.03% expense ratio.
QQQM: Invesco data shows Nasdaq-100 exposure with a 0.15% total expense ratio.
SCHD: Schwab states SCHD tracks a dividend-quality index and uses fundamental strength criteria with a 0.060% expense ratio.
Berkshire Hathaway: 2025 annual report shows insurance operations with large cash, U.S. Treasury bills, equity securities, and negative-cost float in recent years.
Microsoft: FY2025 annual report shows revenue around $281.7B and net income around $101.8B, backed by software, cloud, and AI demand.
Amazon: 2025 results show Q4 net sales up 14%, AWS sales up 24%, and strong operating income growth.
NVIDIA: FY2026 results show revenue of $215.9B, up 65%, with data center revenue as the main AI infrastructure engine.

holdings.name: Vanguard S&P 500 ETF
holdings.moat: Owns a broad basket of the largest U.S. companies at very low cost.
holdings.fundamentalRead: This is the base because it captures U.S. corporate earnings without betting the whole account on one company.
holdings.whyOwn: If I had to pick one holding for a new investor, this is the anchor.
holdings.risk: It can still fall hard in recessions and is concentrated in mega-cap technology.
holdings.reviewRule: Keep unless fees rise materially or a better low-cost S&P 500 ETF replaces it.
holdings.buyPlan: Start with $1,000 now, then add $1,000 every month for 3 more months.

holdings.name: Invesco Nasdaq 100 ETF
holdings.moat: Owns many dominant Nasdaq leaders across software, semiconductors, cloud, consumer internet, and innovation.
holdings.fundamentalRead: Adds more growth exposure than the S&P 500 while avoiding a single-stock bet.
holdings.whyOwn: This is the controlled way to lean into long-term technology growth.
holdings.risk: More volatile than VOO and can lag badly when growth stocks sell off.
holdings.reviewRule: Keep as a growth satellite, not as the whole portfolio.
holdings.buyPlan: Start with $500, then add $500 twice more.

holdings.name: Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF
holdings.moat: Rules-based basket focused on dividend sustainability and fundamental strength.
holdings.fundamentalRead: Balances the growth-heavy ETFs and stocks with quality/value exposure.
holdings.whyOwn: Helps the account feel less like one giant tech trade.
holdings.risk: Can underperform when mega-cap growth dominates the market.
holdings.reviewRule: Keep if the low-cost quality-dividend process remains intact.
holdings.buyPlan: Start with $500, add the remaining $500 later.

holdings.name: Berkshire Hathaway
holdings.moat: Insurance float, cash discipline, operating businesses, and permanent capital culture.
holdings.fundamentalRead: Berkshire is less exciting than AI stocks, but the balance sheet and diversified earnings make it a long-term stabilizer.
holdings.whyOwn: This is the stock I would use as the portfolio's adult in the room.
holdings.risk: Leadership transition and huge size can slow future returns.
holdings.reviewRule: Keep while capital allocation stays disciplined and insurance strength remains intact.
holdings.buyPlan: Buy $500 first, then add $500 after the next market pullback or monthly buy date.

holdings.name: Microsoft
holdings.moat: Enterprise switching costs, Office, Azure, Windows, security, GitHub, LinkedIn, and AI distribution.
holdings.fundamentalRead: Microsoft combines high-margin software, cloud growth, and massive free cash flow better than almost any large company.
holdings.whyOwn: This is the cleanest individual business quality pick in the pack.
holdings.risk: AI spending may pressure margins and valuation can get expensive.
holdings.reviewRule: Review if cloud growth breaks, margins collapse, or AI investment stops producing durable demand.

holdings.name: Amazon
holdings.moat: Scale in logistics, Prime ecosystem, AWS, marketplace network effects, and advertising data.
holdings.fundamentalRead: Amazon has multiple engines: retail efficiency, AWS, ads, subscriptions, and AI infrastructure demand.
holdings.whyOwn: This is the long runway pick with several ways to win.
holdings.risk: Retail margins, antitrust pressure, and AWS competition can hurt returns.
holdings.reviewRule: Review if AWS weakens for several quarters or retail cash generation deteriorates.

holdings.name: NVIDIA
holdings.moat: CUDA ecosystem, GPU leadership, networking, data center scale, and developer lock-in.
holdings.fundamentalRead: The financials are outstanding because AI infrastructure demand is enormous, but expectations are also very high.
holdings.whyOwn: I would own it, but smaller than Microsoft because the stock already prices in a lot of success.
holdings.risk: Semiconductor cycles, export controls, customer concentration, and valuation risk.
holdings.reviewRule: Review if data center growth sharply slows, margins compress, or competitors break the CUDA/software advantage.
holdings.buyPlan: Buy $350 first, then add $350 only after you still want it during volatility.
